I am now on board the Jardine steamer Kung Wo bound for Hankow,
if it ever shoves off. Just now we are anchored about three miles above
Nanking taking on thousands of refugees. I could not get a seat on our
plane from Wuhu to Hankow until Sunday,
so Max and I decided to make
every effort to get on this although we were told every cabin had been
sold, all deck space, and two hundred on the waiting list, but we decided

vehicles apparently had been taken over by the army, but there was
a train that night at 6 P.M. so we got tickets on that. Our party was
now ten, four foreigners and six Chinese. We went to the station
about five thirty and found they were loading troops for the Front.
They were nice looking soldiers from Kwangtung, fairly well-eg nipped,
but very young looking. I ran over to a little shop and bought all
their cigarettes, 40 some packages, and gave then to the soldiers. Max
did the same thing at another shop and after that we really owned the

police escorted us to a private room in the station where we could

The situation in China,
the interior, may become very acute,
and
I think everyone is preparing for a storm. However if my seven years in
China have taught me anything it is that China seems to weather all
storms and return to normalcy in a surprisingly short time. I am interest
ted to see Bix and find out what the latest is. You see they had a dir-
ector's and shareholder's meeting in Nanking while I was in Shanghai. I
was supposed to return to Nanking in time for it, but when the Japanese
surrounded Shanghai I couldn't get back in time..
I didn't call on any
of the Ministry officials when I came through Nanking for the very good
reasons I didn't want to. Mr. Peck told me the results of the meeting

My s trenuous trips of the past ten days have done me a world

keep my head "cut in" and that was what I needed.
